candidate.blueprint_locator: Appendix A, printed p. 26, Safety and Infection Prevention and Control → Standard Precautions/Transmission-Based Precautions/Surgical Asepsis: apply infection-prevention principles and evaluate aseptic technique.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — aseptic urinary-catheter insertion
candidate.educational_objective: Use aseptic technique and the CDC-specified sterile equipment for indwelling urinary-catheter insertion in acute-care hospitals.

options.A: Clean gloves, nonsterile supplies, and a reusable lubricant container because acute-care catheterization uses clean technique.
options.B: Aseptic technique with sterile equipment, including sterile gloves, drape, sponges, an appropriate antiseptic or sterile solution for periurethral cleaning, and a single-use lubricant packet.
options.C: Sterile gloves alone are sufficient; the catheter may contact clean bed linen during insertion if resistance is encountered.
options.D: Clean technique is acceptable in acute care unless the client has recurrent urinary infection or impaired immunity.

candidate.rationale: CDC recommendation II.C states that urinary catheters in acute-care hospitals should be inserted using aseptic technique and sterile equipment. Recommendation II.C.1 specifies sterile gloves, drape, sponges, an appropriate antiseptic or sterile solution for periurethral cleaning, and a single-use packet of lubricant jelly. Clean technique is described as an acceptable alternative for chronic intermittent catheterization in non-acute-care settings, not routine acute-care indwelling-catheter insertion.
candidate.source_claim_supported: CDC requires aseptic technique and sterile equipment for acute-care urinary-catheter insertion and specifies sterile gloves, drape, sponges, appropriate antiseptic or sterile periurethral solution, and a single-use lubricant packet; clean technique is an alternative for chronic intermittent catheterization in non-acute care.
